text: To use the model, convert a program into a graph of small nodes and wires, then repeatedly replace small matching graph pieces.
The model aims for optimal parallel reduction by avoiding work that will later be discarded and reducing necessary work once even when an expression has multiple uses.
Ordinary lambda calculus is compact but leaves open what to do when a variable is unused or appears multiple times.
A lambda node has a binding port for the parameter and a body port for the expression.
If the copied argument still contains redexes, the same necessary work may be repeated in every copy.
densityReasons: Combines copied redexes, repeated work, and per-copy consequence

text: The paper defines ΔL, ΔA, ΔI, and ΔK as corresponding Δ-Net subsystems.
densityReasons: Lists four subsystems and asserts their correspondence

text: Some shared terms have no ordinary sequential reduction order that avoids every duplicated reduction.
densityReasons: Combines shared terms, sequential orders, and universal avoidance failure

text: A shared subgraph should be reduced once so every use observes the result.
densityReasons: Combines shared-subgraph reduction, once-only work, and propagated observation

text: An interaction system is a graph whose small local rewrites can occur independently.
densityReasons: Defines a system using graph structure, locality, and independence

text: An interaction rule rewrites an active pair by reconnecting only the wires attached at that location.
densityReasons: Procedure combines active-pair rewriting, reconnection, locality, and wire scope

text: The pair either disappears or passes through the other, reconnecting only nearby wires. That single application is one interaction step.
densityReasons: Combines disappearance, passage, reconnection locality, and definition of an interaction step.

text: Each agent has one principal port, so two distinct active pairs never share an agent. They can fire at the same time and pick their local rules independently.
densityReasons: Combines principal-port ownership, pair disjointness, simultaneous firing, and independent rule selection.

text: Confluence asks whether different valid reduction choices can disagree. The one-step diamond property is a strong “no”: if a net N has two possible single steps, either choice leads to a net that meets the other after exactly one more interaction.
densityReasons: Defines confluence and the one-step diamond property with competing reductions and their convergence timing.

text: How to read the diamond. Starting at N, choose either available step. The paths meet at M. Every arrow shows exactly one local interaction.

text: The paper calls this perfect confluence. Each active pair owns the only principal port of each of its two agents, so distinct active pairs use distinct agents. Their rewrites commute: left-then-right and right-then-left leave the same nearby wiring.
densityReasons: Combines perfect confluence, port ownership, pair disjointness, commuting rewrites, and wiring locality.

text: The diamond says competing local steps agree. Termination is separate: some nets can reduce forever. The paper’s claim is narrower: when a core interaction order normalizes, every normalizing order reaches the same result in the same number of interactions.
densityReasons: Contrasts local confluence with nontermination and states a qualified normalization-result theorem.

text: Earlier interaction-net approaches tracked sharing scopes—regions governed by one duplication context, the way a λ governs its bound uses. They marked those regions with indexed fans plus extra delimiter agents (brackets, croissants, and kin). The critique is practical as much as theoretical: delimiters pile up, and their interactions can outnumber the useful fan work. Some systems also let indices grow without bound.
densityReasons: Combines sharing-scope motivation, indexed delimiters, practical overhead, interaction cost, and unbounded-index criticism.

text: Δ-Nets folds that bookkeeping into one variable-arity agent—the replicator—with a level and a per-port delta. One structure holds the sharing context.
densityReasons: States the proposed bookkeeping simplification and identifies level, deltas, and unified context storage.

text: A Δ-Net is built from three agents: fan, eraser, and replicator. Think of each as a tiny component. The principal port is the socket that can start a rewrite. The auxiliary ports carry the surrounding wiring through that rewrite.
densityReasons: Introduces three agents and explains principal versus auxiliary port roles.

text: Diagram key. Application and function fans are triangles: the principal port is fixed at the top apex and the two auxiliary wires leave fixed, symmetric positions along the bottom edge. Only replicators are trapezoids: the principal port is centered on the short top side and the auxiliary wires are evenly spaced along the wide bottom side. Rectangles label fragments or wire endpoints; they are not agents. An eraser has only a principal port.
densityReasons: Combines visual conventions for multiple agent types, port placement, wire spacing, fragment labels, and eraser structure.

text: Exactly two auxiliary ports. Fans build the application and abstraction skeleton of a λ-term. When two fans annihilate, that is β-reduction in graph form.
densityReasons: Combines fan arity, term-structure role, and correspondence between fan annihilation and beta reduction.

text: No auxiliary ports. It marks “this bound variable is unused,” and deletes an agent it meets in a distinct-agent interaction.
densityReasons: Combines eraser arity, unused-variable meaning, and deletion behavior.

text: Any natural-number arity—one, two, three auxiliary ports, and so on. It joins the uses of one shared value and records the sharing context: a level on the agent, plus a delta on each auxiliary port.
densityReasons: Combines variable arity, sharing role, and level-plus-delta context representation.

text: The integer level names the replicator’s sharing context. Each auxiliary port carries an integer delta. A replica that leaves through a port adds that delta to its current level—like a signed offset stamped on the exit door.
densityReasons: Defines level and port deltas and explains their arithmetic effect on replica levels.

text: In plain language: linear means exactly one bound use, affine at most one, relevant at least one, and full any count. The split mirrors the paper’s opening taxonomy and shows which agent pays for which feature: fans for structure, erasers for omission, replicators for sharing.
densityReasons: Combines four usage definitions with the agent-feature correspondence and taxonomy rationale.

text: Formally, equal replicators must match in level, arity, and every port delta. For well-formed nets from the paper’s λ-term translation, active replicators at the same level are already equal—so an implementation may compare levels alone in that setting. Hand-built nets do not get that shortcut.
densityReasons: Combines formal equality criteria, a well-formed-net shortcut, and its limitation for hand-built nets.

text: Parent and child are direction labels on a wire. In a rooted net, a parent points toward the root and a child points away from it—think “who faces whom,” not family trees. Canonical nets start with unpaired fan-in replicators: auxiliaries are parents, principal is a child. Reduction can also create fan-outs, with that orientation flipped. A fan-out is paired upstream with at least one fan-in; a fan-in need not have a partner. Levels and deltas let you reason about that pairing locally.
densityReasons: Combines orientation definitions, rooted-net interpretation, canonical structure, reduction-created inversions, pairing constraints, and local level-delta reasoning.

text: The interaction rules are the engine. This chapter groups their wire reconnections into three families: cancellation, deletion, and passage-with-copying. Each name describes what happens to one active pair.
densityReasons: Introduces interaction rules and classifies them into cancellation, deletion, and passage-with-copying.

text: Equal agents cancel. In a well-formed net from a λ-term, active replicators at the same level are equal: both nodes disappear and matching auxiliary ports reconnect. For fans, that same cancellation is applying a λ to its argument.
densityReasons: Combines equality conditions, well-formed-net qualification, reconnection behavior, and fan-to-beta-reduction interpretation.

text: An eraser is distinct from its neighbour and has zero auxiliary ports, so the agent it meets has nowhere to continue through. It is deleted.
densityReasons: Combines distinctness, zero-arity reasoning, lack of continuation, and deletion outcome.

text: Distinct non-eraser agents pass through each other. How many outgoing copies you get depends on the other agent’s auxiliary ports.
densityReasons: States passage behavior and relates copy count to auxiliary-port count.

text: Why erasure propagates. Distinct agents pass through one another once per auxiliary port. Because E has zero auxiliary ports, the fan produces zero surviving copies; because the fan has two auxiliary ports, two copies of E continue into M and N. An n-port replicator would analogously leave n erasers. This is the erasure family from [the paper’s core interaction rules](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20314v4#S2.F4).
densityReasons: Combines propagation mechanism, port-count causality, generalization, and citation.

text: Applications and abstractions are both fans. You tell them apart by how their wires point when you look from the root—the unique top entry of the whole net. When the right pair of fans meets principal-to-principal, they annihilate: both nodes go away and matching auxiliary ports reconnect. Auxiliary ports are ordered clockwise when the principal port points down; flipping one fan upside down swaps its visible left and right, so the wires cross in the drawing. That is β-reduction at the net level.
densityReasons: Combines fan interpretation, root orientation, annihilation, port reconnection, geometry, and beta-reduction.
Diagram encodes application-abstraction structure, port labels, orientation, and principal connection.
Diagram represents two indexed reconnections and their resulting pairings.

text: The crossing is structural. For the downward application fan, the left auxiliary is first and the right auxiliary is second. For the rotated upward abstraction fan, the right auxiliary is first and the left auxiliary is second. Matching first-to-first and second-to-second—not geometric sides—therefore crosses the wires.
densityReasons: Combines port ordering, fan rotation, visible geometry, matching semantics, and wire crossing.

text: When a replicator meets a fan, the replicator leaves through the fan’s two auxiliary ports as two exact copies. At the same time, the fan leaves through every auxiliary port of the replicator—one fan per port. Each keeps its role, but now sits in the other’s surrounding context.
densityReasons: Combines two replication directions, cardinalities, role preservation, and contextual placement.
Diagram encodes a three-port replicator, two-port fan, principal interaction, and auxiliary wiring.

text: Finite version of the paper’s fan–replicator rule. Port identities, not geometric sides, determine the reconnection: (Fᵢ)ⱼ ↔ (Rʲ)ᵢ. This guide-specific diagram uses a three-port replicator so every copy has a visible port and wire. It adapts the structure of [Figure 4 in the source paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20314v4#S2.F4) (CC BY 4.0).
densityReasons: Combines formal rule, port-index semantics, diagram-specific arity choice, adaptation, and licensing citation.

text: Count both sides. R has three auxiliary ports, so three fans F₀, F₁, F₂ appear. F has two auxiliary ports, so two replicators R⁰, R¹ appear. Because F points upward, its clockwise auxiliary-port order is visible right-to-left: a₁ is on the left and a₀ is on the right. Thus the old visible-left a₁ wire remains attached to R¹, while the old visible-right a₀ wire remains attached to R⁰; those two outer wires do not cross. Internally, auxiliary port j of each new Fᵢ connects to port dᵢ of Rʲ.
densityReasons: Combines port counting, orientation, index order, outer-wire preservation, crossing behavior, and internal reconnection.

text: First compare the two levels. If they match—and the net came from a well-formed λ translation—the replicators are equal: they annihilate, both nodes disappear, and matching auxiliary ports reconnect. No replicas are created. In a hand-built net, matching levels alone are not enough; arity and every port delta must match too.
densityReasons: Combines equal-level annihilation, well-formedness assumptions, and additional arity and delta constraints.

text: If the levels differ, the replicators are distinct and commute. Call the lower-level one R and the higher-level one H. R makes one replica of H for each of R’s auxiliary ports; H makes exact copies of R for each of H’s ports. Each H replica takes the delta on its exit port through R and adds it to H’s current level. The second diagram shows that different-level case.
densityReasons: Combines unequal-level classification, two replication directions, level transformation, and exit-port behavior.

A delta may be negative, zero, or positive; this example sticks to zero and a positive value only to keep the arithmetic easy to see.

text: For each of λL, λA, λI, and λK, the paper defines a bijection φ from terms to canonical Δ-Nets. A bijection is a one-to-one, reversible map: every term has one canonical net, and that net reads back as one term. The translation is inductive: translate the smaller pieces first, then wire those fragments into the larger term.
densityReasons: Combines four calculi, bijection properties, canonicality, reversibility, and inductive construction.

text: The vocabulary used by the translation. λx.M defines a function; x is its parameter and M is its body. M N applies function M to argument N. In the example, A is the actual argument supplied to the abstraction, while x₀ and x₁ are the two places that use x.
densityReasons: Defines multiple lambda-calculus terms and explains several roles in the example.

text: Every fragment has an interface: one incoming wire at the top and zero or more outgoing wires at the bottom. The outermost fragment hangs from a single root. Free variables—names no surrounding λ owns—become named interface nodes. That stable shape lets you plug a fragment into its parent the way a function plugs into a call.
densityReasons: Combines interface shape, root structure, free-variable handling, and compositional motivation.
Diagram encodes ports, ownership, body, variable replicator, and bound uses.

text: Canonical fragment interface. In the abstraction, the parent enters λ’s principal port; λ’s right auxiliary reaches body M, while its left auxiliary reaches the replicator’s principal port when x is shared. In the application, function M reaches the application’s principal port; the parent/result wire and argument N use its two auxiliary ports.
densityReasons: Compresses canonical interfaces for both abstraction and application with port ordering and connectivity.

text: A variable free in the outermost term becomes a single-port, non-agent node labelled with its name. It sits on the net’s interface, not among the rewriting agents.
densityReasons: Explains free-variable representation, interface placement, and exclusion from agents.

text: A bound occurrence is just a vertical wire. Its lower end later joins an auxiliary port of the sharing replicator—when sharing is required at all.
densityReasons: States wire representation and conditional connection to a sharing replicator.

text: The distinction is at the fragment boundary. A free variable survives as a named node in the canonical net’s interface. A bound occurrence introduces no variable agent at all: it is a wire whose endpoint is later connected to its owning λx, directly when there is one use or through Rx when that value is shared. This follows the two variable clauses in [the paper’s inductive translation](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20314v4#S3.F5).
densityReasons: Contrasts free and bound variables, describes boundary representation, and gives direct versus shared wiring with citation.

text: An abstraction is an upward-pointing fan (the λ label is only visual). Its first auxiliary port is the body and its second auxiliary port is the bound variable; in this upward view, those appear on the right and left respectively. If that variable is unused, the second auxiliary port meets an eraser—only in the erasure-capable systems ΔA and ΔK.
densityReasons: Combines abstraction geometry, port semantics, unused-variable behavior, and system-specific erasure qualification.

text: When a used variable has several occurrences, a replicator joins the abstraction’s variable port to those uses. Each auxiliary port of R lands on a concrete use site: for λx.x x, one auxiliary meets the application’s argument port and the other meets its function port. The application itself hangs from the abstraction’s body port. A one-port replicator with zero delta is just a wire, so canonical construction leaves it out.
densityReasons: Explains replicator necessity, port-to-use mapping, a concrete application example, and wire omission for one use.
Diagram represents abstraction ports, one bound use, and their direct wiring.
Diagram combines unused binder behavior, erasure, body connection, and a free variable.
Diagram combines abstraction, application, result wiring, sharing replicator, and two variable-use connections.

text: Read each picture from its λ binder. The second auxiliary port is the bound parameter x: it closes directly to one occurrence, terminates at E when unused, or reaches R when several occurrences must share one incoming value. The first auxiliary port is the body. In λx.x x that body port meets the application’s result port; the replicator’s auxiliary ports meet the application’s function and argument ports. §5.7 adds the levels and deltas.
densityReasons: Provides reading strategy, three binder cases, port semantics, example wiring, and a cross-reference.

text: An application is a triangular fan (the app label is only visual). Its principal port is fixed at the top apex and meets the function fragment. Its result and argument auxiliary ports are fixed symmetrically along the bottom edge. During reduction the application fan eventually meets an abstraction fan; their principal-port annihilation is the application.
densityReasons: Defines application geometry, all port roles, reduction interaction, and principal-port annihilation.

text: Calculate levels by walking the written λ-term. Start the whole term at level 0. For an abstraction λx.M at level ℓ, continue into M at the same level ℓ. For an application M N at level ℓ, keep level ℓ on the function M and write level ℓ + 1 on the argument N. Repeat inside each subtree. During graph reduction those coordinates track sharing contexts; they do not count captured values or surrounding λ symbols the way a runtime closure would.
densityReasons: Gives recursive level-assignment rules and contrasts graph coordinates with runtime closure semantics.

text: - Write level 0 on the whole term, then walk inward. Keep the current level through every λx.M body and every function position; add one only when you enter an application’s argument.
densityReasons: Combines initial labeling, traversal, lambda propagation, function propagation, and argument increments.

text: - For each binder λx at level l, put its sharing replicator Rx at level l + 1 when a replicator is needed.
densityReasons: One construction instruction with conditional replicator placement and level arithmetic.

text: - Connect each bound occurrence xi to one auxiliary port of Rx. If that occurrence was reached at level li, label its port di = li − (l + 1).
densityReasons: Combines occurrence-to-port wiring, occurrence levels, and delta computation.

text: A wire endpoint level is simply the level of that concrete variable occurrence. Its port delta is the gap between where the occurrence sits and where its binder’s replicator sits:
densityReasons: Defines endpoint levels and explains delta as a relational gap.

text: That is where Chapter 4’s numbers came from: a replicator at level 2 wired to an occurrence at level 5 stores delta +3. During reduction, that +3 is the local adjustment whenever another replicator exits through the port. Section [5.8](#deep-deltas) works the full calculation for four occurrences of one bound variable.
densityReasons: Connects a numerical example, reduction semantics, and a section-specific extension to multiple occurrences.

text: The rules feel less abstract when one small program stays on screen the whole way. Start with the closed linear term (λx.x)(λy.y). Each bound variable occurs once, so this is a ΔL example: fans only—no eraser, no replicator.
densityReasons: Combines an example, an explanatory motivation, a linearity condition, and a classification of net agents.

text: How to read the wiring. The downward @-fan’s first auxiliary port is the application result (the root reaches it); its principal port leads to the function; its second auxiliary port leads to the argument. The upward λ-fan’s first auxiliary port is its body and its second auxiliary port is its bound variable. Since the body and variable ports of λx.x are already joined, annihilating the two principal ports connects the root directly to λy.y.
densityReasons: Compresses wiring conventions for two fan types, port roles, an existing connection, and the result of annihilation.

text: The [Katharos diagram for λx.x x](https://zicklag.katharos.group/_astro/lam-x-xx.excalidraw.394327a5_ZJMpfg.webp) is useful because the extra structure is visible: γ nodes carry λ/application shape, and the δ node splits one bound input x into two uses. That image uses symmetric interaction combinators, not Δ-Net notation itself. The map below is conceptual: each γ role becomes a Δ-Net fan; the binary δ becomes a two-port replicator R.
densityReasons: Combines an external diagram interpretation, a notation caveat, and a conceptual mapping from gamma and delta nodes to Delta-Net agents.
Diagram combines abstraction ports, replicator structure, application wiring, levels, and endpoint roles.

text: What the numbers mean in this exact term. The application hangs from the λ body port: its first auxiliary is the result. One replicator auxiliary meets the application’s argument port; the other meets its function (principal) port. The outer term has level 0. The body application is also level 0; the application rule puts the argument occurrence at level 1, while the function occurrence stays at level 0. The replicator belongs to the surrounding abstraction, so it has level 0 + 1 = 1. Therefore its function-use port stores d0 = 0 − 1 = −1, and its argument-use port stores d1 = 1 − 1 = 0.
densityReasons: Combines port interpretation, term levels, application rules, replicator placement, and two stored delta calculations.

text: A level delta is not a copy count, and it is not a source-level variable value. The two-port replicator already says “one bound value, two consumers.” Level and per-port deltas only record the relative sharing context at each consumer. When replicators later commute through structure, those deltas adjust the levels of replicas leaving through their ports. That bookkeeping is how Δ-Nets express the sharing a δ would introduce—without separate scope-delimiter agents.
densityReasons: Distinguishes deltas from copy counts and values, then explains their bookkeeping role during commutation and their relation to delta sharing.

text: The previous term has only one application, so its two use sites differ by a single level. A clearer closed term is λx. x (x (x x)). The parentheses matter: each successive occurrence on the right sits inside another application’s argument, and every argument edge adds one to the term level.
densityReasons: Combines a limitation of the prior example, a new term, nesting interpretation, and a level-increment rule.
Diagram encodes nested application structure, four replicated uses, port roles, and level placement.

text: Why the vector grows. The outer application hangs from the λ body port. Each inner application hangs from the argument port of the application above it. The four replicator auxiliaries meet the three function ports and the deepest argument port. The abstraction is at level 0, so its replicator is at level 1. The four bound-variable endpoints are at levels 0, 1, 2, 3. Applying di = li − lR yields ⟨−1, 0, +1, +2⟩.
densityReasons: Combines nested wiring interpretation, four-use accounting, level assignments, endpoint levels, and a vector calculation.

text: Apply this abstraction to a term N and the replicator stands for four consumers of that one argument. When later interactions move sharing through the nested applications, exits through the four ports adjust an arriving replica’s level by −1, 0, +1, or +2. The numbers keep track of where each use belongs. They still do not say how many copies to make.
densityReasons: Combines application behavior, consumer interpretation, later interaction effects, and the conceptual meaning of the numbers.

text: The full algorithm is more than the interaction core. It adds canonicalization—cleanup rewrites that restore the special term-like net shape—and, for the nonlinear systems, a global leftmost-outermost schedule.
densityReasons: Combines the interaction core with canonicalization, cleanup rewrites, term shape, and scheduling requirements across systems.

text: Translation produces a canonical net: the standard shape the reverse translation knows how to read. After zero or more core interactions you have a proper net—any intermediate shape reachable during reduction. Canonicalization is the cleanup that walks a proper net back to canonical form.
densityReasons: Defines canonical and proper nets, explains their generation and reachability relation, and states the role of canonicalization.

text: Canonical | Directly produced by the φ translation and in the special normal shape the back-translation expects. | It is the stable, term-like representation. | |
densityReasons: Combines a formal state definition, its translation origin, its back-translation role, and reader significance.

text: In ΔA and ΔK, an eraser can leave disconnected subnets—smaller graph regions—behind. Erasure canonicalization gathers that unreachable material in one reachability sweep:
densityReasons: States the problem caused by erasers and introduces the global reachability-based cleanup solution.

text: Run the sweep at the end, or earlier to save space. When memory matters most, the paper recommends it after every application of an abstraction that ignores its argument.
densityReasons: Combines two scheduling options, their space trade-off, and a recommendation conditioned on memory pressure.

text: This is a global cleanup pass, not a principal-port interaction. The sweep begins at the distinguished root, marks the graph material reachable through the parent–child wiring, and deletes everything else. Where deleting an unmarked node exposes a connection that remains in the net, that connection is terminated by E. The schematic follows the erasure canonicalization described in [Section 4 of the paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20314v4#S4).
densityReasons: Combines the cleanup classification, traversal origin and relation, deletion behavior, exposed-wire handling, and paper provenance.

text: In ΔI and ΔK, interactions can build trees made only of replicators. A merge rule collapses consecutive replicators once a local level test shows they are unpaired. Pairing information stays intact; the tree gets shorter.
densityReasons: Combines the systems affected, the structure produced by interactions, the merge condition, and the preservation and purpose of pairing information.

text: For consecutive replicators A and B joined through a port with delta d, B is known unpaired when 0 ≤ lB − lA ≤ d. In the paper’s reading, B cannot interact before A is annihilated—and since A is unpaired, that never happens. The inequality is a safety proof, not a performance hint.
densityReasons: Combines setup, a formal inequality, its unpairing interpretation, an interaction-order argument, and a safety conclusion.

text: The inequality establishes safety; endpoint levels determine the new numbers. Here A is known unpaired, and its connecting port has d = 3. Since 0 ≤ lB − lA = 2 ≤ 3, B is also known unpaired and the consecutive agents may merge. The surviving replicator keeps level 2; the external endpoint levels remain 2, 3, 6, so the new deltas are ⟨0, +1, +4⟩.
densityReasons: Combines the safety rationale, inequality evaluation, merge conclusion, preserved levels, and recomputed delta vector.

text: ΔK has one more cleanup: unpaired replicator decay. Drop auxiliary ports of unpaired replicators that lead straight into erasers. If one zero-delta port remains, the replicator collapses to the wire it already was.
densityReasons: Combines a cleanup procedure, a port condition, and a collapse consequence.

text: Decay removes only eraser-bound auxiliary ports. In this ΔK example, the two E-bound exits contribute no surviving consumers, so they are deleted. The remaining one-port replicator has delta 0; by the canonical representation rule it carries no information beyond the connection itself and collapses to a wire. The paper applies this cleanup during erasure canonicalization or lazily just before relevant replication rules.
densityReasons: Combines decay scope, example-specific deletion, delta interpretation, canonical collapse, and timing alternatives.

text: Core interaction rules enjoy local confluence. Canonicalization can touch ports that are not a principal-to-principal pair, so it needs a schedule. Leftmost-outermost first picks an outermost reducible pattern—one with no reducible pattern wrapped around it—then takes the leftmost candidate in the term-like reading of the net. “Sequential” here just means that priority rule chooses the next interaction. The paper uses that order for ΔA, ΔI, and ΔK so cleanup runs early and merges beat later commutations.
densityReasons: Combines confluence, scheduling motivation, ordering semantics, subsystem scope, and optimization rationale.

text: Important nuance. The paper also permits a reducible pair to run early if it will eventually reach the leftmost-outermost position unchanged. This preserves some safe parallelism while retaining the schedule’s optimality rationale.
densityReasons: Combines an early-execution condition, preservation rationale, parallelism, and optimality.

text: The paper’s final claim is an algorithm for optimal parallel λ-reduction: translate a term to a canonical net, reduce with the core rules plus the required cleanups and schedule, then read the canonical net back as a term.
densityReasons: Combines translation, canonicalization, reduction, readback, and an optimality claim.

text: Keep the state changes separate. The bijection φ creates the initial canonical net. Core interactions enter the broader space of proper nets; the subsystem’s prescribed interaction order and canonicalizations are collected by Ω until the net is both normal and canonical. Only then does φ−1 read it back as a λ-term. This is the construction formalized near the end of [Section 4 of the paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20314v4#S4).
densityReasons: Distinguishes several state spaces and transitions, assigns responsibilities to φ, Ω, and φ⁻¹, and cites the formal location.

text: Leftmost-outermost reduction avoids evaluating a subnet that will later be erased; the reachability sweep clears the leftover garbage.
densityReasons: Combines evaluation-order behavior with a reachability cleanup consequence.

text: Replicators put shared use in the graph, so necessary work need not be redone merely because an expression has several consumers.
densityReasons: Combines the mechanism of graph sharing with the consequence of avoiding repeated work.

text: Perfect confluence in the interaction core lets disjoint active pairs choose and apply their local rules independently.
densityReasons: Combines confluence, disjointness, rule choice, and independent application.

text: In ΔL, fan annihilation is the only interaction. The paper states that every proper net is already canonical, and that if n β-reductions normalize a λL term, n interactions normalize its ΔL encoding in any order. ΔA, ΔI, and ΔK add canonicalization for erasure and sharing structure.
densityReasons: Compares ΔL with nonlinear subsystems and combines interaction counts, order independence, and multiple canonicalization concerns.

text: ΔL | None beyond fan annihilation. | Any interaction order; perfect confluence. | |
densityReasons: States a subsystem property and its prescribed reduction response.

text: ΔA | Discarded subnet garbage. | Leftmost-outermost annihilations + erasure canonicalization. | |
densityReasons: Combines a garbage concern with a specific ordering and canonicalization response.

text: ΔI | Replicator trees and early copies. | Leftmost-outermost + unpaired merging / canonicalization. | |
densityReasons: Combines replicator behavior with ordering, merging, and canonicalization responses.

text: ΔK | Both garbage and sharing context. | Leftmost-outermost + erasure, merge, and decay canonicalizations. | |
densityReasons: Combines two concerns with ordering and three distinct canonicalization mechanisms.

text: - Expressiveness: every term in the four λ fragments has a canonical net, via a stated bijection.
densityReasons: States an expressiveness claim and its bijection-based justification.

text: - Local behavior: the three-agent core is an interaction system with the one-step diamond property.
densityReasons: Combines a system characterization with a one-step diamond property.

text: - Whole-algorithm behavior: add canonicalization and the global schedule, and the paper claims Church–Rosser confluence and optimality for the nonlinear systems. Church–Rosser is the broader agreement property: paths that start together can be continued to a common result—not necessarily in one step.
densityReasons: Combines three claim layers, added mechanisms, global properties, optimality, and a qualification about Church–Rosser.

text: The split matters. The third layer needs erasure sweeps, replicator merging, decay, and leftmost-outermost scheduling on top of the core rules.
densityReasons: Lists multiple mechanisms required for the whole-algorithm claim and contrasts them with core rules.

text: The paper invites you to see λ-calculus as a projection of Δ-Nets. λ-terms force a narrow form of sharing; nets can say sharing relationships that plain syntax hides. If the reduction machinery holds up, that freedom could matter for parallel runtimes and machine architectures.
densityReasons: Combines a projection thesis, syntax-versus-net expressiveness, a conditional premise, and runtime implications.

text: Δ-Nets tries to make optimal parallel evaluation practical by packing each sharing context into a variable-arity replicator, then combining local interactions with only as much global discipline as you need to avoid preventable work.
densityReasons: Combines representation, sharing, local interaction, global discipline, and the practical goal.
